Nirṇayasindhu
------------------------------------------
The Nirṇayasindhu of कमलाकर भट्ट (early part of the 17th century) is an authoritative and voluminous work on the धर्मशास्त्रस् belonging to the class of निबन्धस् or digests.
Kamalākara भट्ट was the son of रामकृष्ण भट्ट and a grandson of नारायण भट्ट, both of whom were also great scholars. Being a person of profound erudition, कमलाकर भट्ट authored several works—more than twenty-two—of which, the Nirṇayasindhu is one and perhaps, his master-piece. The other two works considered as equally famous are: Śūdrakamalākara and Vivādatāṇḍava.
The Nirṇayasindhu is said to be an exposition of कुमारिल भट्ट’s (8th cent. A. D.) Vārttika on Mīmāṁsā. However it is an encyclopaedic work on the धर्म-śāstra subjects, divided into three paricchedas or sections.
A brief account of the contents may now be given:
On divisions of time and the right times for the performance of various rites and vratas; the various सṁस्कारस् or sacraments; consecration of images; auspicious times for various religious actions; śrāddha; rites for सṁन्यास.
It is interesting to note that the work describes the procedure for सती or self-immolation of a widow who willingly undertakes it.
It is equally interesting and educative to learn from कमलाकर’s another work, the Śūdrakamalākara, the various facilities and freedom given to the शूद्रस्, the last of the four varṇas or castes, regarding the worship of gods, observance of vratas or religious vows, allowing at least ten सṁस्कारस् (sacraments), the performance of the पञ्चमहायज्ञस् (five daily sacrifices) and many other socio-religious rites.

nirupādhika
(‘without upādhis [or limiting adjuncts]’)
------------------------------------------
An उपाधि, normally translated as a ‘limiting adjunct’, is an object that makes another object appear to be different from what it actually is, though neither of them really affects each other. For instance, when a red hibiscus flower is kept near a transparent crystal, this crystal appears red, though in reality, it is not! So, the hibiscus flower is an उपाधि for the crystal.
Similarly the आत्मन् (the सोउल् or the Self) inside the body appears to be bound by the limitations or characteristics of the body-मिन्द् complex which is its उपाधि.
Also, ब्रह्मन् (God, the Absolute), appears as responsible for the च्रेअतिओन्, sustenance and destruction of this world, though He is not.
In reality, in both these cases, neither the आत्मन् nor ब्रह्मन् is affected by the upādhis of the body-मिन्द् complex or the world appearance. Hence they are called ‘nirupādhika,’ ‘without the upādhis’ or ‘unaffected by the upādhis’.

nīrājana
(‘[waving of] water or light’)
------------------------------------------
Ritualistic worship of God in and through an icon (either at home or in a temple) is a common feature in हिन्दुइस्म्. The various उपचारस् (items of honour) are a part of this. They remind one of the way one has to receive an important guest visiting one’s होउसे.
Such उपचारस् may be five (pañcopa-cāras), ten (daśopacāras) or sixteen (ṣoḍa-śopacāras). In all these, waving of a lighted lamp called ‘nīrājana,’ is a must. It may be of burning karpūra (camphor) or cotton wicks dipped in ghee or oil, their number being 3 or 5 or 7.
Some आगमस् declare that by such waving of light, one’s life and happiness increase and all evil beings are driven out.
Sometimes, coloured water kept in a shallow plate is waved before a sick person, to ward off the evil forces that might have caused the disease. This is also called ‘nīrājana’ (nīra = water).

Nirṇayasāgara Press
------------------------------------------
The printing of the Hindu scriptural works in the देवनागरी (Sanskrit) script has always been an arduous task. When the printing presses were still in the early stages of development, much more care was needed to get the final product right. The निर्णयसागर प्रेस्स् is one printing press that deserved all praise.
Started in A.

, it was situated at the following address: 26-28, Kolbhat Street, Bombay-2. It was one of the oldest commercial organisations of India, totally dedicated to the printing and publication of Sanskrit books. Apart from the well-known Hindu scriptures it had brought out the literary works also under the Kāvyamālā series.

nirayana
(‘neglecting the precession of the equinoxes’)
------------------------------------------
An equinox is the point where the sun crosses the plane of the earth’s equator. There are two equinoxes: the vernal equinox (on March 21) and the autumnal equinox (on September 22). On these two days, the length or the duration of the day and the night are exactly equal.
In the traditional Hindu calendars (called ‘pañcāṅgas’) the precession of the equinoxes (due to the wobbling movement of the earth) is not taken into account. Hence this system of calculation is known as निरयन whereas, if taken into account, it is called sāyana.
Though the actual date of the vernal equinox at present is 21st March, it is considered as 13th April ignoring the precession.
In order to remove this anomaly, the National चलेन्दर् (as recommended by the चलेन्दर् Reform Committee) was adopted in 1957. March 22 was reckoned as the 1st चैत्र, Śaka-era 1879. The duration of the year adopted for calculations taking the अयन or precession into account (hence ‘sāyana’) was 365.2422 days.

nirvicārasamāpatti
(‘samādhi [on subtle objects] without discrimination’)
------------------------------------------
The words समापत्ति and समाधि mean the same thing: attaining (mentally) the object of concentration, or perfect concentration on the object of concentration.
While dealing with समापत्ति, the Yogasūtras (1.42-44), has mentioned four types of them: savitarka and nirvitarka; savicāra and nirvicāra.
Out of the aṣṭāṅgas or eight steps described by the Yogasūtras, the last three—dhāraṇā, ध्यान and samādhi—are clubbed together and given the technical name ‘saṁyama’ (vide 3.4).
When सṁयम is practised on the subtle elements of the object comprising it and only the subtle object of concentration shines before the मिन्द्’s eye, all other processes being completely transcended, it is called ‘nirvicāra समापत्ति’.

nirvikalpaka
(‘without distinctions’)
------------------------------------------
Samādhi or total absorption in ब्रह्मन् is of two kinds: सविकल्पक and निर्विकल्पक. विकल्प means distinctions, the चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of the many like ‘me’ and ‘Brahman’ and the world. In the सविकल्पक समाधि the चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of one’s own personality as distinct from ब्रह्मन्, persists, however attenuated it may be. In the निर्विकल्पक state, however, all awareness of multiplicity including that of oneself as distinct from ब्रह्मन्, is completely dissolved.

Nirūḍhapaśubandha
------------------------------------------
Animal sacrifices were quite common during the days of Vedic yajñas. The निरूढपशुबन्ध was one such. It could be done as a part of सोमयाग or even independently.
The procedure seems to have been reconstructed by the authors of the śrauta-sūtras from the original material available in the ब्राह्मणस्.
It was to be performed by an आहिताग्नि (one who had established Vedic fires) either twice or once a year.
A he-goat was the animal prescribed for immolation, the deities being इन्द्र, अग्नि, सूर्य and प्रजापति. Six priests were needed for its performance.
See also VEDIC SACRIFICES.

nirmāṇacitta
(‘mind created [by the योगि]’)
------------------------------------------
The Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) contains some startling revelations, one of them being the ‘nirmāṇacitta’ (vide 4.4 and 5).
When a योगि is advanced very highly in the spiritual path, he discovers through his intuitive inner eye, that he still has some सञ्चितकर्म about to fructify as प्रारब्धकर्म. This can delay his kai-valya or लिबेरतिओन्. Hence, using his special yogic powers he can create simultaneously a few suitable bodies through which he can experience and exhaust this कर्म. The चित्त or the मिन्द् in each of the bodies thus created, is called ‘nirmāṇa-चित्त’.
Patañjali makes it clear that though each of these nirmāṇacittas acts differently through the different bodies to exhaust that कर्म, the original or basic चित्त is that of the योगि, which controls them.

Nirīśvara-sāṅkhya
(‘the Sāṅkhya philo-sophy that does not accept ईश्वर or God’)
------------------------------------------
The philosophies of Sāṅkhya and योग are generally studied together. Whereas the former concentrates on the metaphysical side, the latter pays the maximum attention to sādhanā or spiritual practice that ultimately leads to कैवल्य or लिबेरतिओन्.
Whereas the Sāṅkhya propounds 25 cosmic principles behind च्रेअतिओन्, the योग accepts all of them and then adds ईश्वर or God as the 26th principle. Since the former school does not accept ईश्वर or God, it is called ‘Nirīśvara-sāṅkhya’ (nir = not). The latter, as opposed to it, is termed ‘Seśvara-sāṅkhya’.
See SĀṄKHYA DARŚANA and YOGA DARŚANA for details.

nirviśeṣa
(‘that which is without special characteristics’)
------------------------------------------
The nature of the highest Reality, generally designated by the word ‘Brahman’ in the उपनिषद्स्, is an important point of discussion in the Vedānta philo-sophy, considered as the crest-jewel of Indian philosophical systems.
According to the Advaita Vedānta, ब्रह्मन् has two lakṣaṇas or characteristics; तटस्थलक्षण (accidental characteristic) and स्वरूपलक्षण (intrinsic characteristic).
When ब्रह्मन् is described as responsible for the च्रेअतिओन् or evolution of this world (vide the Brahmasūtras

) it is the first lakṣaṇa that has been indicated. This is only an indirect way of pointing towards it.
However, in its own intrinsic nature it is described as ‘nirviśeṣa-cinmātra-svarūpa’.
It is pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् without any viśeṣas or qualities. It is this essential nature of ब्रह्मन् that is indicated by the word ‘nir-viśeṣa’ (= without specific qualities). Another word used in the same sense is ‘nirguṇa’ (vide Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11).
See also SVARŪPALAKṢAṆA and TAṬASTHALAKṢAṆA.

------------------------------------------

nirgarbha
(‘without the womb [of the मन्त्र]’)
------------------------------------------
Prāṇāyāma or control of the prāṇic energy through the control of breath is an important aspect of the aṣṭāṅgayoga of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.). It has three steps: पूरक (infilling of air into the lungs), कुम्भक (retention of breath) and रेचक (exhalation).
The कुम्भक has eight varieties of which the first is ‘sahita’. This again is of two types: सगर्भ and निर्गर्भ.
When the प्राणायाम is performed using the बीजमन्त्र (seed-letter prescribed for the same) it is called ‘sagarbha’. If done without it, it is called ‘nirgarbha’. कुम्भक being a part of it, is also called by the same name.
See PRĀṆĀYĀMA for details.

Nirṛti
(‘[deity of] unfailing misfortune’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘Nirṛti’ occurs for the first time in the Ṛgveda (10.165.1) as an evil spirit, as a personification of sin.
Jyeṣṭhādevī or अलक्ष्मी is also sometimes called निरृति. (See ALAKṢMĪ for details.)
However, निरृति is more commonly pictured as the guardian deity presiding over the south-western direction. He is one of the eight दिक्पालकस् (guardian spirits of the quarters).
Iconographical works describe him as dark in colour, with a huge body and matted hair. He has two hands carrying a sword and a shield. Caṇḍikā or Rākṣaseśvarī is his consort. He rides on a donkey.
Of course, there are other descriptions also.
An अवकीर्णिन् (a brahmacāri who has violated the vow of chastity) was expected to sacrifice an ass to appease निरृति as an atonement for the sin.
There are other Nirṛtis also mentioned in the पुराणस्.
He is one of the eleven Rudras.
As a woman, she is the wife of अधर्म (unrighteousness). Bhaya (fear), Mahābhaya (great fear) and मृत्यु (death) are her offsprings (vide Ādiparva of the Mahābhārata,
Ch. 67

nirodha-samādhi
------------------------------------------
This is the same as NIRBĪJA-SAMĀDHI. See the same for details.

nirbījasamādhi
(‘samādhi in which the seed of rebirth is destroyed’)
------------------------------------------
This is a term specially used in the Yogasūtras (1.51) of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.).
The chief reason for सṁसार or transmigration is the impurity of the मिन्द्. These impurities, through their सṁस्कारस् or tendencies carried over many births, impel the मिन्द् to constantly rise in the form of vṛttis or modifications, preventing a vision of the पुरुष or the आत्मन् who is asaṅga (detached) and चैतन्य (pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्), established in our hearts.
When the aṣṭāṅgayoga (yoga of eight graded steps) as recommended by पतञ्जलि is practised, the योगि experiences समाधि (superconscious state) wherein ऋतम्भरप्रज्ञा (truth-bearing knowledge or wisdom)—which is practically the same as ātmajñāna—arises. As this knowledge prevents and destroys all other modifications of the मिन्द् (vide 1.48-50), निर्बीजसमाधि (a समाधि wherein all karmas that would have caused rebirth are destroyed at the root itself) results. Then the योगि becomes a mukta or liberated.

Nirukta
(‘etymology’)
------------------------------------------
The वेदस् are the basic scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्. A correct understanding of the same is necessary not only for knowing their philosophy but also for the performance of the innumerable rites associated with them.
To facilitate this, the वेदाङ्गस् or the six subsidiary limbs of the वेदस् were composed by competent ṛṣis or sages. The Nirukta is one of them.
Actually, the Nirukta is a commentary on the Nighaṇṭu, a lexicon of Vedic words and terminology, of hoary antiquity.
Yāska the author of this work lived probably during 800 B. C. Hindu tradition however, pushes this date back to 2000 B. C.
Since the Nirukta is actually a gloss on the Nighaṇṭu, which itself is a kind of Vedic dictionary, it can be considered as the earliest Vedabhāṣya (commentary on the वेदस्).
The Nirukta contains 14 adhyāyas or chapters. Leaving the last two as परिशिष्ट or appendices, the rest—the first twelve chapters—is divided into pūrvaṣaṭka and uttaraṣaṭka, each containing six chapters.
The first chapter is introductory.
The next five chapters (2 to 6) deal exhaustively with the Naighaṇṭuka and the Naigama Kāṇḍas of the Nighaṇṭu.
The seventh chapter, again, is an introduction to the subject of the Daivata-kāṇḍa of the Nighaṇṭu.
The next five chapters (8 to 12) give detailed etymologies and explanations of the names of the Vedic deities.
The last two chapters (13 and 14) contain eulogies of the Vedic deities and spiritual teachings and instructions.
The contents of the entire work may be summarised very briefly thus: several points of Sanskrit grammar; the theory that all words are derived from dhātus or verbal roots; all mantras have specific meanings and usages; the need to know the deity of the mantras; in praise of those who know the meaning of the mantras; ways of deriving the meanings of words; explanations of the words of the Nighaṇṭu; characteristics of a Vedic मन्त्र; power of the mantras and the deities; meditating on the forms of the deities; definitions of the deities of the earth, हेअवेन् and intervening space and so on.
The Nirukta throws a lot of light on the contemporary life of the society. Sanskrit was the spoken language. There were earlier treatises on this subject as also grammar. The sweep of the subjects dealt with or referred to, reveals the wide and deep scholarship of the author यास्क. He supported the theory that all words were derived from verbal roots and has proved it in a highly scientific and systematic manner.
There are two commentaries on the Nirukta, one by Durgācārya (before A.
) and the other by two scholars, स्कन्दस्वामिन् and महेश्वर who lived sometime during the period A.
and A.

.
See also NIGHAṆṬU.
